idiom_name: Kind struct value shared through a pointer field; map[string]*Kind registry
implementation_notes: Go has no classes at all, so the paper's TypeClass/Class pair becomes two structs and a registry: a Kind struct holds the shared type data, a Monster holds *Kind plus its own state, and a map[string]*Kind loaded from JSON is the type table. Behaviour that varies per kind is a function field on Kind (or an interface value) rather than a virtual method, which keeps the kind table data-driven. reflect.Type, Go's built-in representation of types, is comparable and usable as a map key, but it describes the program's own types and cannot carry your fields, so it is the runtime's type system, not your type object. For a closed set of kinds an interface plus concrete types (or a typed enum switch) is simpler and checked by the compiler.
pitfalls: A map registry shared across goroutines must be synchronised (sync.RWMutex or atomic.Pointer to an immutable map); plain map reads racing with registration crash the program.
Storing the kind by value (Monster{kind Kind}) copies the type data into every instance and breaks pointer identity checks such as m.kind == kinds["troll"]; keep the pointer.
Adding fields to Kind after instances exist silently gives old instances zero values for them; version the type data and construct kinds once, before any monster is spawned.
